sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
July 2026 delivered a sharply bifurcated global equity tape underpinned by a single dominant force: the re-escalation of U.S.-Iran military hostilities on July 7-8, which reversed the post-ceasefire oil normalization and injected a stagflationary shock into an already policy-sensitive market environment. The S&P 500 closed the month essentially flat at **7,489.72**, masking extreme sector dispersion; the energy sector gained **+12.1%** while technology shed **-8%**, producing the widest monthly sector gap in over three years.

American large-cap indices diverged sharply. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **+0.6%** to **52,485.03** — its fourth consecutive monthly advance — driven by energy, financials, and healthcare, while the Nasdaq Composite declined approximately **-2%** (approx., verify before merging) to **25,373.85** as mega-cap technology underwent significant de-rating ahead of and despite a broadly strong Q2 earnings season. Europe and APAC diverged even more dramatically: Germany's DAX advanced approximately **+4.8%** (approx., verify before merging) while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell approximately **-8.7%** (approx., verify before merging) to **64,362.02**.

The MSCI All Country World index finished July up a modest **+0.1%**, with foreign developed markets the only major asset class to post clearly positive returns (**+1.98%**). The month's defining dynamic was a rotation away from AI/growth concentration — which had powered 2026's first-half advance — toward value, energy, and dividend-yielding sectors, a regime shift that portfolio managers expect to persist into H2 2026 as oil-driven inflation reinforces the Federal Reserve's hawkish hold.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
Middle East Re-Escalation & the Crude Oil Supply Shock -- The most consequential geopolitical event of July 2026 was the breakdown of the U.S.-Iran ceasefire and escalation of military hostilities on July 7-8, which immediately reversed the oil price normalization that had been the dominant macro tailwind entering the month. Brent crude surged from approximately **$76/bbl** at end-June to approximately **$92/bbl** by July 31 (approx., verify before merging), a gain in excess of **+20%** that represented the benchmark's best monthly performance in over two years. WTI tracked higher to approximately **$84/bbl** (approx., verify before merging), with both benchmarks touching intra-month highs near **$99/bbl** before retracing as U.S. naval escorts provided intermittent Strait of Hormuz passage.

The oil supply shock delivered an immediate stagflationary impulse to an economy already navigating elevated Federal Reserve vigilance. Airlines, chemical producers, and logistics companies — many of which had aggressively reduced crude hedges on the June ceasefire news — faced severe near-term margin compression. Energy sector equities registered their best global monthly performance since 2022, with the U.S. energy sector alone gaining **+12.1%** for July while European integrated oil majors posted double-digit monthly advances.

For financial markets, the re-escalation materially complicated the H2 2026 macro narrative. The Strait of Hormuz — through which approximately a fifth of global oil flows — remains partially disrupted, and any further deterioration in negotiations could push Brent back toward **$100/bbl**, a threshold that would likely force a Federal Reserve policy response and trigger a more abrupt de-rating of equity multiples. The IEA revised its global oil demand forecast for H2 2026 upward by **0.4 million barrels per day**, assuming sustained supply disruption will require strategic petroleum reserve releases by consuming nations.

Amazon Blowout & the Big Tech Earnings Divergence -- Amazon's July 30 Q2 2026 results delivered one of the most consequential single-stock earnings reports in recent memory: net revenue of **$200.6 billion** — the company's first quarter exceeding the **$200 billion** threshold — on earnings per share of **$5.75**, dramatically ahead of sell-side consensus of **$1.81**. AWS cloud revenue surged **37%** year-over-year to **$42.2 billion**, its fastest quarterly growth rate in 18 quarters, as AI inference workloads and enterprise cloud migrations drove demand well above expectations. Amazon shares jumped approximately **+15%** on July 31, propelling the company's market capitalisation above **$3 trillion** and providing the decisive boost that rescued the S&P 500 from a materially deeper monthly drawdown.

The blowout occurred against a backdrop of investor anxiety about AI capital expenditure sustainability across the hyperscaler complex. Amazon guided full-year 2026 capex to **$220 billion** — approximately **+50%** above 2025 levels — while collective AI infrastructure commitments from the four major cloud operators exceeded an estimated **$500 billion** for the year. Markets are increasingly pricing a scenario where AI infrastructure investment will not generate commensurate revenue returns for multiple quarters, which contributed directly to the Nasdaq's monthly underperformance despite a broadly constructive earnings season.

Sector bifurcation was the earnings season's defining characteristic: S&P 500 operating earnings growth for Q2 2026 tracked **+15%** year-over-year, yet the technology sector declined **-8%** for the month as investors punished forward capex guidance and questioned AI monetisation timelines. The divergence between Amazon's stock reaction and the broader tech tape reflects a maturing phase of the AI investment cycle where individual winners are being differentiated from the broader infrastructure buildout narrative, with free cash flow conversion emerging as the key variable separating market outperformers from underperformers.

Federal Reserve Hawkish Hold and Rising September Hike Risk -- The Federal Reserve's July 28-29 FOMC meeting produced a divided decision to hold the federal funds rate at **3.50%–3.75%**, with three committee members dissenting in favour of an immediate **25 basis point** hike — the largest dissent count in Chair Kevin Warsh's tenure. Warsh's post-meeting remarks introduced hawkish language acknowledging that supply-side inflationary pressures from energy dislocations and tariff pass-through posed upside risk to the **2%** inflation target. CME FedWatch subsequently priced a greater than **61%** probability of a rate hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting.

U.S. Treasury yields reacted sharply: the 10-year note finished July at **4.75%**, rising approximately **+25 basis points** over the month, while the 2-year yield climbed to **4.28%**, producing a 10-2 spread of **+47 basis points** as the curve modestly steepened. Real yields on 10-year TIPS moved above **2.3%** — a level that historically creates meaningful headwinds for equity multiples in technology and other long-duration sectors. Rate-sensitive sectors including REITs, utilities, and consumer staples meaningfully underperformed the broader index as the repricing propagated through financial conditions.

For asset allocators, the prospect of a hiking cycle resumption in September — barely one quarter after the prior policy pivot had been absorbed — introduces the risk of a more aggressive tightening trajectory than consensus had assumed entering H2. The Fed's central dilemma remains unchanged: an energy-driven supply shock is inherently stagflationary, punishing real growth while simultaneously demanding a policy response that further tightens financial conditions. Chair Warsh's continued revision of the Fed's communication framework — shorter statements, elimination of forward guidance, pure data dependence — adds uncertainty premium to an already complex signal environment.

Copper Tariff Implementation and Industrial Metals Disruption -- The Trump administration's **50%** Section 232 tariff on semi-finished copper imports, which reached full enforcement in July, generated significant front-loading dynamics as market participants raced to secure pre-tariff inventory. More than 200,000 tonnes of copper arrived at U.S. ports during the month — the largest monthly inflow since 2014 — driving COMEX inventories to record levels and creating a structural premium between COMEX and LME pricing. COMEX copper settled near **$6.38/lb** on July 29 (approx., verify before merging), up approximately **+3.3%** (approx., verify before merging) for the month and **+43.6%** year-to-date, as tariff arbitrage, AI data centre construction demand, and South American supply disruptions converged to tighten physical balances.

The tariff's full implementation exposed a structural complexity beyond the headline rate: the shift from taxing copper metal content to taxing the full declared value of fabricated products — including fabrication costs, logistics, and embedded margin — represents a materially higher effective burden than the nominal rate implies. Copper-intensive industries including electrical equipment manufacturing, HVAC systems, and renewable energy development are actively restructuring procurement chains, with several major utilities and data centre developers reporting build schedule delays due to input cost escalation.

The COMEX-LME premium stood at approximately **19 cents per pound** in late July — roughly eight times its 2005-2025 historical average — signalling that U.S. buyers are pricing sustained tariff enforcement rather than treating the measure as temporary. For industrial investors, the copper story encapsulates a broader commodities theme of 2026: the intersection of structural demand growth from AI infrastructure and energy transition with supply-side constraints imposed by both geology and trade policy, creating an extended period of elevated industrial metals pricing with significant second-order implications for manufacturing margins globally.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equity performance in July 2026 was defined by an intensifying divergence between value-oriented large-caps and growth-heavy technology names, as the oil supply shock and rising rate expectations drove a sector rotation that reshaped index-level returns. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **+0.6%** to **52,485.03** — its fourth consecutive monthly advance — led by energy names, diversified financials benefiting from rate repricing, and healthcare which provided a defensive bid. The S&P 500 ended essentially flat at **7,489.72**, though the quiet headline concealed extraordinary cross-sectional dispersion: the equal-weight S&P 500 outperformed the cap-weight version materially as energy (**+12.1%**) and financials (**+6.2%**) dominated while technology (**-8%**) weighed on aggregate index returns.

The Nasdaq Composite bore the heaviest losses, declining approximately **-2%** (approx., verify before merging) to **25,373.85** as a wave of de-risking in long-duration growth names preceded and initially overshadowed the Q2 earnings season. Concerns centred on AI capital expenditure sustainability — collective capex guidance from the four major hyperscalers for 2026 exceeded **$500 billion** — and whether infrastructure investment at this scale could be justified by near-term AI revenue returns. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index names were particularly volatile, oscillating around Nvidia and TSMC guidance updates that shaped appetite for the AI infrastructure theme.

The decisive turning point came on July 31 when Amazon's blowout Q2 report — **$200.6 billion** in revenue, AWS growth of **37%**, and EPS of **$5.75** — catalysed a broad rally that lifted the S&P 500 by more than **+1%** on the final trading day, effectively rescuing the index from a materially deeper monthly drawdown. The month's outcome — a fourth consecutive Dow gain, the Nasdaq's worst month in over a year, and an S&P 500 ending flat despite extraordinary intra-month volatility — is the clearest signal yet that equity leadership is rotating away from mega-cap growth toward value, energy, and dividend-yielding sectors.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets outperformed their U.S. growth-heavy counterparts in July 2026, with energy sector strength and resilient industrial earnings driving positive regional returns. Germany's DAX gained approximately **+4.8%** (approx., verify before merging) to close near **26,126** (approx., verify before merging), led by integrated oil majors, chemicals, and machinery exporters that benefited from the crude surge even as trade policy uncertainty cast a shadow over export-oriented manufacturing. The FTSE 100 advanced approximately **+2.1%** to close near **10,888**, supported by heavy energy and mining sector weighting, while France's CAC 40 advanced approximately **+0.9%** (approx., verify before merging) with mixed sectoral outcomes as luxury goods and automotive names faced headwinds.

The re-escalation of U.S.-Iran hostilities proved a structural tailwind for European large-cap indices given their significantly heavier energy sector weighting relative to U.S. benchmarks. BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, and ENI collectively posted double-digit percentage gains in July, accounting for a disproportionate share of regional outperformance. European defence names continued their structural advance — geopolitical instability renewed procurement momentum for Airbus, Rheinmetall, and BAE Systems — as NATO member defence budgets were revised upward in the wake of the Middle East escalation.

Not all European sectors benefited equally: automotive stocks declined on U.S. tariff uncertainty, with German OEMs particularly exposed to new trade framework measures covering the vast majority of U.S. trade partners. European banks were mixed — the prospective September Fed rate hike provided a net interest margin tailwind for cross-border operations, but oil-driven inflation raised consumer credit quality concerns in Southern Europe. The ECB maintained its policy rate unchanged at its July meeting, signalling it would monitor energy price pass-through before adjusting its own normalisation path. The broader STOXX Europe 600 declined approximately **-0.2%** (approx., verify before merging), reflecting the drag from sectors outside the energy and defence complex.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered a sharply negative performance in July 2026, with Japan and China moving under distinct but intersecting macro pressures. Japan's Nikkei 225 declined approximately **-8.7%** (approx., verify before merging) to close at **64,362.02** — its worst monthly performance in over a year — as the Bank of Japan's increasingly hawkish signals on potential rate normalisation strengthened the yen and compressed the export-earnings multiple that had underpinned the index's exceptional year-to-date advance. A regional technology rout in semiconductor names added further pressure to an already-fragile sentiment backdrop strained by rising global bond yields.

China was the clear regional laggard. The Shanghai Composite fell approximately **-5.2%** (approx., verify before merging) — its worst monthly decline in over a year — pressured by U.S. tariff escalation covering the vast majority of trade partners, consecutive months of Caixin manufacturing PMI export-order contraction, and continued property sector deleveraging. The Hang Seng tracked broadly lower, closing near approximately **25,858** (approx., verify before merging) as declines in China technology and consumer names weighed on the benchmark. The PBOC cut the reserve requirement ratio for select banks mid-month but refrained from broader stimulus, disappointing markets pricing more aggressive easing given the deteriorating trade and growth outlook.

The Bank of Japan's July meeting was the most closely watched event for the region: while the BOJ refrained from an immediate rate hike, revised policy language strongly implied normalisation before year-end 2026. USD/JPY approached approximately **161** (approx., verify before merging) as the initial yen-strengthening impulse proved insufficient to sustain appreciation against a dollar still supported by higher U.S. real yields. The prospective narrowing of the U.S.-Japan rate differential is a structural shift for global carry trades and regional FX volatility, and represents a key risk variable for Japanese equity returns for investors who have benefited from yen-denominated hedging dynamics through H1 2026.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
Currency markets in July 2026 were shaped by the interaction of three competing forces: geopolitical risk-driven demand for U.S. dollar safe-haven assets, the inflationary impulse of higher crude oil prices, and growing expectations of a September Fed rate hike. The DXY dollar index traded in a relatively tight range, touching an early-July high near **101.4** before settling back to approximately **99.9** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end — down approximately **-1.6%** (approx., verify before merging) for the month as the immediate geopolitical risk premium faded and the euro partially recovered on Europe's terms-of-trade improvement from energy sector strength.

EUR/USD held near approximately **1.14** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end, with the euro benefiting from European current account improvements while the ECB's July hold limited rate-differential widening that had pressured the pair earlier in H1 2026. GBP/USD traded near approximately **1.34** (approx., verify before merging), supported by resilient UK labour market data and the Bank of England's continued hold. The most significant developed-market FX move was in the Japanese yen: USD/JPY approached approximately **161** (approx., verify before merging) as BOJ hawkish signals proved insufficient to drive sustained yen appreciation against a dollar supported by higher U.S. real yields, while yen carry-trade positioning remained crowded and vulnerable to further BOJ language shifts.

Emerging market currencies experienced broad-based pressure in July, with CNY, INR, and MXN all weakening as tariff escalation triggered capital outflows from EM assets. The Chinese yuan's controlled but persistent depreciation reflects official tolerance for a weaker exchange rate as a partial offset to export volume losses from trade restrictions. EM central banks in commodity-importing economies faced a particularly acute policy trade-off: defending currencies against a weak domestic growth backdrop while import inflation from higher energy prices eroded real household purchasing power — a constraint that limits their ability to ease policy in response to slowing growth.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
July 2026 was defined almost entirely by the crude oil market and the geopolitical events that drove it. Brent crude surged from approximately **$76/bbl** at end-June to approximately **$92/bbl** by July 31 (approx., verify before merging) — a gain in excess of **+20%** representing the benchmark's best monthly performance in over two years — following the U.S.-Iran hostilities escalation on July 7-8 that triggered immediate Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions. WTI crude advanced commensurately to approximately **$84/bbl** (approx., verify before merging), with both benchmarks touching intra-month highs near **$99/bbl** before retracing as U.S. naval escorts and alternative routing partially alleviated the supply shock. Goldman Sachs sharply revised its Q3 2026 Brent forecast upward to **$95/bbl**, reversing the **$80/bbl** target set following June's peace framework.

Gold settled near approximately **$4,082/oz** as of July 30 (approx., verify before merging) — near record levels — supported by safe-haven demand, rising inflation expectations, and sustained central bank accumulation. The relative underperformance of gold versus crude oil reflects the competing headwind of higher real Treasury yields: with 10-year TIPS yields above **2.3%**, the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion remains elevated. Copper gained approximately **+3.3%** (approx., verify before merging) for the month to settle near **$6.38/lb** (approx., verify before merging) on July 29, driven by AI data centre construction demand and physical front-loading ahead of tariff enforcement, bringing its year-to-date gain to approximately **+43.6%**.

The commodity complex delivered its strongest aggregate monthly performance in over two years, driven overwhelmingly by energy. For corporate earnings, the crude oil move has two distinct second-order effects: a material earnings acceleration for energy producers globally, and simultaneous margin compression on airlines, shipping companies, chemical producers, and consumer goods manufacturers that will crystallise in Q3 2026 guidance downgrades. The IEA revised its global oil demand forecast for H2 2026 upward by **0.4 million barrels per day**, assuming sustained supply disruption will require strategic petroleum reserve releases by consuming nations.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
U.S. Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher in July, as oil-driven inflation expectations and rising September rate-hike probability combined to push the curve upward across tenors. The 10-year Treasury note finished July at **4.75%**, rising approximately **+25 basis points** over the month, while the 2-year yield settled at **4.28%** — producing a 10-2 spread of **+47 basis points** as the curve modestly steepened. The steepening reflects a market increasingly pricing near-term rate stability alongside elevated long-term inflation risk from structural energy market disruption and tariff pass-through.

The Federal Reserve's decision to hold at **3.50%–3.75%** was expected, but Chair Warsh's commentary signalling upside risk to the **2%** inflation target from energy and tariff dynamics fundamentally shifted the terminal rate distribution. Fed funds futures ended July pricing a greater than **61%** probability of a **25 basis point** hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting — a dramatic reversal from the rate-cut expectations prevailing in the spring. Real yields on 10-year TIPS moved above **2.3%**, creating headwinds for long-duration equity multiples and driving underperformance in REITs, utilities, and consumer staples. The prospective September hike also drove a meaningful widening in 30-year mortgage rates, further dampening the housing market recovery that had begun in Q1 2026.

Credit markets showed early signs of stress: investment grade corporate spreads widened by approximately **+15 basis points** (approx., verify before merging) and high yield by approximately **+40 basis points** (approx., verify before merging) over the course of the month, as energy-driven inflation and rate-hike risk combined to pressure leveraged balance sheets and increase refinancing risk for lower-rated issuers. European sovereign spreads — particularly Italian BTPs — widened modestly on oil price inflation pass-through concerns. For fixed income allocators, the July repricing suggests a regime where neither the short nor the long end provides a clear safe harbour, and active duration management will be a key performance differentiator through H2 2026.
